Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Ship Captain
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Object Throwing: Throwing objects, Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drop Responsibilities: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers, Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences

Vignette:
Jerome, a 42-year-old ship captain, had spent two decades commanding vessels across open waters, trusted by crews and owners alike. That changed on a winter night three years ago, when a faulty fuel line—one he had reported twice to the shipping company—ignited during a cargo transfer at a busy port. The explosion ripped through the starboard side of his container ship, killing two deckhands and injuring four others. Jerome was thrown against the bridge console; a heavy toolbox toppled from a shelf and struck his shoulder. In the chaos, he saw the coast guard arrive in their dark blue uniforms, shouting orders he could barely hear over the ringing in his ears. For days afterward, investigators questioned him. He cooperated fully, but the company’s legal team deflected blame, and no charges were ever filed. The families of the dead men sued privately, but Jerome heard nothing more. He was cleared of wrongdoing, but he could not shake the certainty that the people who had cut corners and ignored his reports had simply walked away.

In the months that followed, Jerome began to change. He found himself flinching whenever a crew member tossed a rope or a duffel bag across the deck. The sight of any uniform—security guards at the port gate, police officers on the dock—sent a cold wave through his chest. And bangs: a hatch slamming, a forklift backfiring, even the sound of a truck hitting a pothole near his home—each one made him duck, heart pounding, certain that another explosion was coming. He started to avoid thinking about the event altogether. If a colleague mentioned the accident, he changed the subject or walked away. He had come to believe that if he let himself dwell on it, he would unravel completely, and there would be no putting himself back together.

His marriage, once steady, began to fray. Jerome stopped discussing his work with his wife, Sarah. He felt a deep, unspoken conviction that he could not rely on other people—not the company, not the investigators, not even Sarah, who tried to comfort him but could not understand. He began to drop responsibilities at work, delegating safety inspections to his first mate and declining assignments that would take him to unfamiliar ports. “I can’t assess the danger,” he told himself, though he never said it aloud. At home, he insisted on sitting with his back to a wall in restaurants, always choosing a booth where he could see the door. At night, he lay rigid in bed, listening for sounds that might signal a threat, often staying awake until dawn.

To cope with the constant tension, Jerome turned to gambling. He started with small online poker games, then moved to sports betting and blackjack. The risk and the rush offered a temporary escape from the intrusive images and the ache in his shoulder. He told himself it was just a way to feel something other than fear, but the losses mounted. Sarah found credit card statements and confronted him. He could not explain why he did it; he only knew that when the cards were dealt, he did not have to think about the explosion, the uniforms, the toolbox flying toward his head.

By the time Sarah insisted he see a therapist, Jerome was barely functioning. He had taken indefinite leave from his captain’s post, claiming he needed time off. His sleep was fractured by nightmares of fire and the sharp crack of metal tearing. He could no longer walk into a grocery store without scanning every face for potential danger. What frightened him most was the thought that the world would never feel safe again—that the people who caused the disaster had gone unpunished, and that he was alone in carrying the weight of what happened. He came to the first session not knowing what he wanted, only that he could not go on like this. He hoped, maybe, that someone might finally believe him, and that somewhere in the telling, the hold of the past might loosen.
